EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN ― BORDER-DISCONTINUITY × DIFFERENCE-IN-DIFFERENCES DESIGN

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Method: Spatial border–discontinuity Difference-in-Differences (BD-DiD) with an event-study extension.

Rationale
• Spatial RDD alone compares counties straddling a border at a point in time, but many policy variables (e.g., right-to-work) change within states over the sample period.  
• A two-way fixed-effects DiD applied within matched border pairs exploits both the geographic discontinuity (to get similar counterfactuals) and the time variation in policy adoption (to purge time-invariant cross-state differences).  
• The event-study specification allows us to test pre-trend (parallel trend) assumptions.

Formally,

y_{cst} = β Policy_{st} + γ_c + δ_t + θ_{pair} + X_{cst}′π + ε_{cst}

where γ_c = county FE, δ_t = year FE, θ_{pair} = border-pair FE. Counties are indexed by c, their state by s, year by t.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable
Policy_{st}: indicator (or continuous rate) for a policy in state s and year t. We will estimate separate models for:
• Right-to-work (RTW) law in force (=1 after effective date)  
• Corporate income tax rate (continuous)  
• Targeted manufacturing incentives (binary or dollar amount)

Control group
Counties whose adjacent cross-border neighbor was treated but which themselves are in a state without the policy at time t provide the contemporaneous control.

Treatment timing
For binary laws (RTW) the event date is the calendar year in which the law becomes effective. For tax rates we treat the magnitude in each year as continuous exposure.

Running variable / cutoff
Although the design is not a pure RDD, distance-to-border will be measured (in km from county centroid) and the analytic sample is restricted to counties ≤ 50 km from a state border. This keeps treated and control units locally comparable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends within border pairs  
In the absence of the policy change, manufacturing outcomes in adjacent counties would have moved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Adjoining counties share labor markets, infrastructure, and local demand, supporting similar trends.

A2. No significant cross-border policy spillovers (SUTVA)  
The policy mainly affects the treated side; any effect on the control side is second-order.  
Plausibility: Some firm relocation across the border is the mechanism of interest. We assume net effects on the control county do not fully offset, but we will test for negative spillovers.

A3. Exogeneity of policy timing relative to border-pair shocks  
Policy adoption is driven by statewide politics, not by shocks specific to border counties.  
Plausibility: Reasonable for RTW laws and broad tax changes that reflect partisan shifts rather than county-specific lobbying.

A4. Stable composition of counties  
No large annexations or border changes; manufacturing establishments correctly assigned to counties.  
Plausibility: U.S. county borders are stable; Census data track establishments reliably.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Pre-existing divergent trends   
Mitigation: Event-study leads; control for county-specific linear time trends; placebo tests with pseudo-treatments.

T2. Concurrent policy bundles (e.g., tax cuts + infrastructure grants)  
Mitigation: Include vector of other state-year policies; estimate stacked DiD where each policy is isolated; perform difference-in-difference-in-differences (DDD) using non-manufacturing sectors as additional controls.

T3. Spatial spillovers / relocation undermining SUTVA  
Mitigation: Estimate symmetric effects on control side; run model on progressively narrower distance bands (50 km, 25 km, 10 km). If treatment coefficients attenuate with distance while control-side coefficients grow, spillovers are evident; report net effect across both sides.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline (executable)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE and event studies
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three csv files: counties.csv, policies.csv, borders.csv
# counties.csv: county_id, state, year, manuf_emp, manuf_plants, covariates...
# policies.csv: state, year, rtw, corp_tax, manuf_incentives
# borders.csv: county_id, border_pair_id, dist_to_border_km

cty <- fread("counties.csv")
pol <- fread("policies.csv")
bd  <- fread("borders.csv")

# 2. Merge and Create Analysis Sample -------------------------------------
data <- merge(cty, pol, by = c("state","year"))
data <- merge(data, bd,  by = "county_id")

# restrict to counties within 50 km of border
data <- data[dist_to_border_km <= 50]

# 3. Key Variables ---------------------------------------------------------
data[, treat_rtw  := rtw]              # binary
data[, l_manuf_emp := log1p(manuf_emp)]# outcome
# create county-pair FE factor
data[, pair_fe := factor(border_pair_id)]

# 4. Main DiD Regression ---------------------------------------------------
m1 <- feols(l_manuf_emp ~ treat_rtw | pair_fe + year + county_id, data)
summary(m1)

# 5. Event Study with Sun & Abraham ---------------------------------------
data[, rel_time := ifelse(treat_rtw==1, year - min(year[treat_rtw==1]), NA)]
# Sun & Abraham coding handled internally by sunab()
m2 <- feols(l_manuf_emp ~ sunab(state, year, treat_rtw) | pair_fe + year + county_id,
            data)
iplot(m2)            # Plot dynamic effects

# 6. Robustness: narrower bandwidth (<=25 km) ------------------------------
rob <- feols(l_manuf_emp ~ treat_rtw | pair_fe + year + county_id,
             data[dist_to_border_km <= 25])
etable(list(Main = m1, BW25 = rob))

# Save results
saveRDS(list(main = m1, event = m2, robustness = rob), "results.rds")
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic intuition suggests right-to-work laws and lower tax rates make a state more attractive to manufacturing.  
Prior: β < 0 for corporate tax (higher tax → lower activity); β > 0 for RTW.  
Magnitude: A new RTW law might raise manufacturing employment by 3-5 percent in treated border counties within 5 years; a 1 pp decrease in the corporate income-tax rate might raise employment by ~0.5 percent.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (for DiD)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1 Parallel pre-trends verified via event-study …………………… 1  
C2 No anticipatory effects (leads ≈ 0) ………………………………… 0.8  
C3 SUTVA / no interference across units ……………………………… 0.5  
C4 No time-varying confounders within border pairs ……………… 0.8  
C5 Data quality & correct treatment coding ………………………… 1  

(Score: 4.1 / 5)

Overall, with careful dynamic diagnostics and bandwidth robustness, the BD-DiD strategy should credibly estimate the causal impact of state policies on the geographic distribution of U.S. manufacturing.
